title: Hasekura Tsunenaga's Embassy to New Spain, Spain and Rome
intro: Hasekura Tsunenaga, a samurai and retainer of Date Masamune, the daimyō of Sendai, headed the Keichō Embassy, a diplomatic mission to Pope Paul V. He went by way of New Spain and visited various ports of call in Europe.
ending: Hasekura returned to Japan in August 1620, reaching the harbour of Nagasaki. European monarchs had refused the trade agreements he sought, and he died of illness a year later.

legs.title: Across the Pacific and New Spain

stops.text: The San Juan Bautista, a ship built for the purpose, left for Acapulco with around 180 people on board, among them samurai of the shōgun and of Sendai, merchants, sailors and about 40 Spaniards and Portuguese.
stops.quote: The Great Ship left Toshima-Tsukinoura for the Southern Barbarians on 15 September Japanese calendar, with at its head Hasekura Rokuemon Tsunenaga

stops.text: The ship sighted Cape Mendocino and continued along the coast of California.
stops.quote: The ship sighted Cape Mendocino on 26 December 1613, continuing along the California coast

stops.text: After three months at sea the delegation arrived and was received with great ceremony. Fights broke out between the Japanese and the Spaniards, especially Vizcaíno, and orders were issued on 4 and 5 March to restore peace.
stops.quote: The delegation arrived at Acapulco on 25 January, after three months at sea. The Japanese were received with great ceremony, but had to wait in Acapulco until orders were received regarding how to organize the rest of their travels.

stops.text: The embassy entered the city and was received with great ceremony. Hasekura was lodged next to the Convent of San Francisco and met the Viceroy, and many of his companions were baptised there in April.
stops.quote: The embassy remained two months in Acapulco and entered Mexico City on 24 March, where it was received with great ceremony.

stops.text: The embassy went to Veracruz to board the fleet of Don Antonio Oquendo. Hasekura left part of his group behind in Mexico, and the fleet sailed for Europe on 10 June.
stops.quote: The embassy spent some time in Mexico, and then went to Veracruz to board the fleet of Don Antonio Oquendo.

stops.text: The embassy stopped in Havana in Cuba and changed ships there. It stayed in the city for six days before going on to Spain.
stops.quote: The embassy stopped and changed ships in Havana in Cuba in July 1614. The embassy stayed in Havana for six days.

stops.text: The fleet arrived safely after some dangers and storms. The Duke of Medina Sidonia was told of its arrival and sent carriages to bring the ambassador and his gentlemen ashore.
stops.quote: The fleet arrived in Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 5 October 1614.

stops.text: Hasekura entered the city accompanied by 30 Japanese with blades, a captain of the guard, and 12 bowmen and halberdiers with painted lances and ceremonial blades.
stops.quote: The Japanese ambassador Hasekura Rokuemon, sent by Joate Masamune, king of Boju, entered Seville on Wednesday, 23 October 1614.

stops.text: Hasekura met King Philip III and gave him a letter from Date Masamune and an offer of a treaty. The king answered that he would do what he could. Hasekura was baptised on 17 February at the Convent of Las Descalzas Reales.
stops.quote: The Japanese embassy met with King Philip III in Madrid on 30 January 1615.

stops.text: Bad weather forced the embassy, sailing on three Spanish frigates towards Italy, to stay a few days in the French harbour. Local nobility received them, and the town's chronicles recorded their visit.
stops.quote: Due to bad weather, they had to stay for a few days in the French harbour of Saint-Tropez, where they were received by the local nobility, and made quite a sensation on the populace.

stops.text: The embassy met Pope Paul V on 3 November and gave him two letters requesting a trade treaty and missionaries. The Pope agreed to send missionaries but left the trade decision to the King of Spain.
stops.quote: The Japanese Embassy arrived at Rome on 20 September 1615 and was received by Cardinal Burgecio; the delegation met Pope Paul V on 3 November.

stops.text: After meeting the king again in April 1616, Hasekura found that he declined to sign a trade agreement. The mission left Seville for New Spain in June. Some Japanese may have stayed behind in villages near the city.
stops.quote: Two years later, after their trip around Europe, the mission left Seville for New Spain (Mexico) in June 1616.

stops.text: The San Juan Bautista reached the Philippines with Hasekura and Luis Sotelo on board. The Spanish government bought the ship, and Hasekura bought goods for Date Masamune and built a ship.
stops.quote: In Manila, the archbishop described the deal to the king of Spain in a missive dated 28 July 1619

stops.text: Hasekura finally returned to Japan, reaching the harbour of Nagasaki after his stay in the Philippines.
stops.quote: He finally returned to Japan in August 1620, reaching the harbour of Nagasaki.

stops.text: Hasekura reported his travels to Date Masamune and gave him a portrait of Pope Paul V and a portrait of himself in prayer. Two days later an edict against Christians was promulgated in the Sendai fief.
stops.quote: Hasekura reported his travels to Date Masamune upon his arrival in Sendai.

notes: Tsukinoura: the date 28 October 1613 is from the Trans-Pacific voyage paragraph, not the quote; the departure port is named 'Toshima-Tsukinoura' in the article's quoted passage; wp points to Ishinomaki, whose harbour the Legacy section names as his departure. Zacatula: wp title may need checking. Veracruz: no date for the stay; 1614 is inferred from the fleet leaving on 10 June (year given only in the Departure paragraph's context). Manila: the article says the ship arrived 'in the Philippines'; Manila is named only for the archbishop's letter, so the point is an inference. Sendai: no year given for the report; 1620 inferred from the August 1620 return. Rome stop: arrival 20 September 1615 as given. Left out: the return across New Spain in 1619 (the article says Hasekura re-traced his route in 1619 yet has him in Manila in April 1618, and he stayed 5 months in Mexico; dates contradict), Coria del Río and Espartinas (named only as last stops, no date or event), Cavite and the 1609 to 1612 earlier voyages (not Hasekura's). The Saint-Tropez date follows the article's 'in 1615' with no day. Sendai edict 'two days later' is from the article's quotation of the edict.
